title: When is a product less than the other number?
description: Two thirds times nine and five halves times nine are worked out and compared with nine. One shrinks nine and the other grows it, and that gives a rule about the number being multiplied. Keeko raises the doubt that both products must be less than nine.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number between zero and one makes the product less than the other number, and a number greater than one makes it greater. Watch for students who think any fraction shrinks the other number, even a fraction that is greater than one.

source: Use 2/3 × 9 and 5/2 × 9 to fill in the blanks: when one numb
video_script.why: A learner sees one rule about the size of a product from two products with the same number nine.
video_script.substitution: the numbers of the book's own fill in the blanks, two thirds, five halves and nine
video_script.anchor: two products of nine, one by two thirds and one by five halves, placed on a number line against nine
video_script.wrong_answer: both products are less than nine
video_script.wrong_move: treats every fraction as a number that shrinks, without checking whether it is greater than one
video_script.payoff_line: The product is less for a number between zero and one, greater for a number above one

final_answer.value: less when a number is between 0 and 1; greater when a number is greater than 1
final_answer.spoken: less for a number between zero and one, greater for a number above one

video_script.fraction_reading: two thirds, five halves, forty five halves
maths_rules: 2/3 is between 0 and 1 and 5/2 is greater than 1
